The NFL Draft is the annual event in which the National Football League selects college football players to join its professional teams. It has been held since 1936 and has evolved into a televised spectacle that determines which players transition to the pros. Draft position, especially the coveted first overall pick, significantly predicts career success and earning potential, making it a focal point of sports media, strategy, and anticipation.

The Draft currently consists of seven rounds with thirty-two teams selecting in reverse order of their previous season's record. The worst team picks first, attempting to create competitive balance, while elite players are selected early and role players and depth selections come later. The first overall pick is the most prestigious selection, and quarterbacks historically dominate early picks. Several first-overall selections have become Hall of Famers, including Joe Montana, John Elway, and Peyton Manning.

Teams can trade their draft picks for future picks or established players. Strategic trading shapes draft outcomes significantly. Some teams package multiple picks together to move up for a desired prospect. The Draft emerged from the NFL's competition with the rival American Football League. The AFL's competition for talent motivated the creation of the first draft. The two leagues merged in 1970 and unified the Draft process.

College football is the primary pipeline for NFL talent. The NFL Draft incentivizes elite college players to enter the pros early, or conversely, to stay through their senior year to improve their draft position. This competition shapes college football coaching and recruitment throughout the nation. Mock drafts—predictions of draft outcomes—are produced by media analysts, and draft analysis has become an entire media industry. Expert commentators, highlight reels, and detailed scouting reports dominate the weeks leading up to the event.

Bust picks occur despite careful scouting. High selections sometimes fail to produce at professional levels. Conversely, sleeper picks from the later rounds can succeed and generate team identity and fan investment. This uncertainty is what makes the Draft so compelling to watch.
